title: Comanche Creek Well Depth and Drilling Cost
meta_description: Comanche Creek wells have a 340-foot median depth, with typical completed-well costs of $23,000-$35,800.
h1: Comanche Creek, Colorado Well and Water Guide
intro_html:
Buying land near Comanche Creek means dealing with Denver Basin groundwater, not a uniform shallow plains aquifer. Records within the local search area show a wide range of well depths, but most completed wells fall in a useful planning range. The same records also show generally productive wells, with a median reported pump yield of 10.0 gallons per minute.

This guide uses Colorado Division of Water Resources permit records near Comanche Creek in Arapahoe County. Use the numbers to frame a driller’s bid and a property inspection, then verify the specific parcel, permit conditions, water quality, and septic layout before closing.

sections.heading: Comanche Creek well depth and the Denver Basin
sections.html:
The median well depth near Comanche Creek is 340 feet. The middle half of reported wells runs from 118 to 381 feet, so a bid near the median is reasonable for planning, but it is not a guarantee for a particular lot. The 90th-percentile depth is 500 feet, and the deepest recorded well reaches 1,046 feet.

Depths cluster in the deeper part of the range: 58% of wells are between 300 and 600 feet. Another 24% are under 100 feet, while 13% fall between 100 and 300 feet and 4% are 600 feet or deeper. The permits name Denver Basin aquifers on all of the Denver Basin wells in this dataset, along with Denver, Arapahoe, and unnamed or fractured-bedrock descriptions.

sections.heading: What a Comanche Creek well is likely to produce
sections.html:
Reported production is one of the stronger parts of this local record. The median pump yield is 10.0 gallons per minute, and the middle half runs from 10.0 to 12.0 gallons per minute. Most reporting wells, 87%, produce between 5 and 15 gallons per minute. Eleven percent report more than 15 gallons per minute.

Only 2% report between 1 and 5 gallons per minute, and none report under 1 gallon per minute. That does not eliminate the possibility of a poor well on an untested parcel. It does mean a buyer can reasonably use 10.0 gallons per minute as a local comparison point when reviewing a well test, pump selection, storage tank, and household demand.

Domestic and household use appears on 75% of permits. Stock use appears on 53%, while irrigation appears on 9%. A permit’s authorized use still controls what the well can legally supply.

sections.heading: Water levels near Comanche Creek
sections.html:
Where static water levels were reported, the median depth to water is 120 feet below the ground surface. The middle half of measurements ranges from 82 to 150 feet. That matters when comparing pump settings, estimating lift, and planning electrical work.

The decade figures deserve a closer look. The median reported water level was 100 feet below the surface in the 2010s and 120 feet in the 2020s. That is a deeper measured level in the newer decade, but it is not enough by itself to prove a basin-wide declining water table. Measurement locations, seasons, well construction, and the smaller reporting subset can all affect the comparison.

Ask for the well’s static level, pumping level, and test details rather than relying only on the area median.

sections.heading: Permit history and drillers in this area
sections.html:
Comanche Creek has a long permit record, with 683 wells in Colorado DWR records and 391 recorded as constructed. Reported depths are available for 427 wells, pump yields for 302, and static water levels for 101. That difference is important: the strongest local statistics come from subsets of the full permit file.

Permit activity was highest in the 2000s, with 237 permits, followed by 125 in the 2010s and 90 in the 2020s. The newest permit year in the records is 2025. Older permits extend back to the 1950s.

Crandall Drilling & Pump Service, including Crandall Jr. and Howard H., appears most often with 213 records. Hamacher Well Works Inc. follows with 61, and Crandall's Look-N-Good Drilling appears with 25. Those are record appearances, not a recommendation or a guarantee of current availability.

sections.heading: Planning the cost of a new Comanche Creek well
sections.html:
The local cost model uses Denver Basin sedimentary bedrock and a drilling rate of $50 to $70 per foot. At the 340-foot median depth, the drilled hole works out to about $17,000 to $23,800. A finished system, including the pump, tank, trenching, and electrical, is estimated at $23,000 to $35,800.

Use that range to compare bids, not as a fixed quote. The final price can change with actual depth, casing and grout requirements, access, trench length, power availability, pump size, storage, and site conditions. A driller should separate the per-foot rate from mobilization, casing, grouting, testing, and completion items.

If a parcel has no existing well, price the full water system before deciding what the land is worth.

sections.heading: Risks to check before building near Comanche Creek
sections.html:
Water quantity looks favorable in the records, but an area average cannot rule out a low-yield or unsuccessful hole. Fractured or variable subsurface conditions can make one lot perform differently from its neighbors. Review nearby well depths, yields, static levels, construction reports, and permits before buying.

Water quality deserves specific attention. Mapped sites within about 10 miles include 40 PFAS sampling or contamination sites and 27 EPA Superfund or cleanup sites. That does not establish contamination at a particular parcel, but it supports testing the existing well and checking the site’s location relative to known environmental records.

Confirm septic setbacks, replacement-area requirements, driveway access, and building envelopes before drilling. A well location that works for water may conflict with septic, drainage, utilities, or a future home.

sections.heading: A practical lot check for Brick Center, Strasburg, and Byers
sections.html:
For a Comanche Creek lot, start with the DWR permit file and compare it with nearby properties in Brick Center, Strasburg, and Byers. Look for wells close in depth and aquifer description, not just the nearest mapped point. The local 340-foot median and 10.0-gallon-per-minute median are useful benchmarks for a preliminary budget and water plan.

Have a Colorado-licensed driller review the parcel before closing if the lot is undeveloped. Ask for a written estimate that addresses access, expected depth, casing, grout, pump equipment, storage, trenching, electrical work, testing, and the possibility of additional depth. If a well already exists, obtain the construction report, permit conditions, water-quality results, pump test, and maintenance history.

Finally, confirm that the permitted use matches your house, stock, irrigation, or other plans. Water rights and augmentation requirements can matter even when a well produces well.

faq.q: How deep are wells near Comanche Creek, Colorado?
faq.a: The median reported depth is 340 feet. The middle half of wells runs from 118 to 381 feet, while the 90th-percentile depth is 500 feet. Most wells, 58%, are between 300 and 600 feet. The deepest record reaches 1,046 feet, so a local median should guide planning rather than serve as a guaranteed drilling depth.

faq.q: How much does it cost to drill a well in Comanche Creek?
faq.a: The local model uses a drilling rate of $50 to $70 per foot. At the 340-foot median depth, the drilled hole is estimated at $17,000 to $23,800. A completed system with pump, tank, trenching, and electrical is estimated at $23,000 to $35,800. Access, final depth, casing, grout, and site conditions can change the quote.

faq.q: How much water do wells near Comanche Creek produce?
faq.a: The median reported pump yield is 10.0 gallons per minute, with the middle half between 10.0 and 12.0 gallons per minute. About 87% of reporting wells produce between 5 and 15 gallons per minute. Two percent report 1 to 5 gallons per minute, and none report under 1 gallon per minute, though a specific new well can differ.

faq.q: Is well water near Comanche Creek safe to drink?
faq.a: The permit records do not establish that every well is safe to drink. About 10 miles of the area includes 40 PFAS sampling or contamination sites and 27 EPA Superfund or cleanup sites. Test an existing or new well through a qualified laboratory, review nearby environmental records, and retest after repairs, flooding, or changes in taste, odor, or appearance.

faq.q: Is the water table dropping near Comanche Creek?
faq.a: Reported median static water level changed from 100 feet below the surface in the 2010s to 120 feet in the 2020s. That indicates deeper measurements in the newer decade, but the record does not prove a basin-wide decline. Only 101 wells report static water levels, and differences in location, season, construction, and measurement conditions can affect the comparison.
